opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing is to be really clear about what the environment looks like, because with tool-using agents the environment *is* the problem in a lot of ways. You need a sandbox where the model can actually call the tools: run code, hit a search API, query a database, whatever it is. And it needs to be fast and reproducible, because RL is going to hammer it with thousands and thousands of rollouts. If your environment is flaky, your reward signal is noisy, and then you're basically training on garbage.

The second thing is the reward. I'm a big believer in starting with verifiable rewards wherever you can get them. If the task has a checkable outcome, like the code passes the tests, the answer matches, the file ends up in the right state, use that. It's much harder to reward-hack than a learned reward model. For more open-ended tasks you might bring in an LLM-as-judge or a rubric, but you have to watch it closely, because the policy will find whatever shortcut the judge allows.

Third, I usually don't start RL from a raw base model. You want some kind of warm start, typically supervised fine-tuning on good trajectories, maybe distilled from a stronger model, so the agent already knows the tool-calling format and roughly how to sequence actions. RL is really good at sharpening behavior that already shows up sometimes. It's not great at discovering a format from scratch when the reward is sparse.

Then there's data and curriculum. You want tasks at the right difficulty. If the model solves everything, or nothing, there's no gradient signal. So we spend a lot of time filtering problems to the band where the pass rate is somewhere in the middle, and refreshing that as the model improves.

On the algorithm side, people mostly use PPO-style methods or GRPO and its variants these days. The details matter, though: how you handle multi-turn credit assignment, masking out the tool outputs so you're not training the model to predict the environment's tokens, managing long contexts as trajectories grow, and keeping an eye on things like entropy collapse.

And finally, honestly, a lot of it is just looking at the rollouts. You read the trajectories, you see the weird things the model is doing, you find the reward hacks, you fix the environment, and you iterate. The infrastructure and the evals end up being where most of the work goes. The RL algorithm itself is almost the smallest part.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that training a tool-using agent with RL is really a systems problem first and an algorithms problem second. People tend to jump straight to the algorithm—PPO, GRPO, whatever—but honestly, most of the hard work is in setting up the environment correctly.

So the first thing we do is get very precise about what the environment actually is. For a tool-using agent, the environment isn't just a prompt and a response. It's a multi-turn interaction where the model emits a tool call, something external executes that call—could be a code interpreter, a search API, a database—and the result comes back into the context. And then the model decides what to do next. So you have this trajectory that can be quite long, with these interleaved model turns and tool outputs, and you have to decide which tokens you're actually taking gradients on. You don't want to be training on the tool outputs, right? Those weren't generated by the policy. So masking those out properly is a basic but surprisingly common place where things go wrong.

The second piece is the reward. The nice thing about tool-using tasks is that a lot of them have verifiable outcomes. If the agent is supposed to write code that passes tests, you run the tests. If it's supposed to answer a question by searching, you can check the final answer against ground truth. So we lean heavily on these outcome-based rewards because they're hard to game and they scale. What you want to avoid, at least early on, is heavy shaping—rewarding the model for calling a tool, or for calling it a certain number of times—because the model will just learn to do that thing rather than solve the problem. We've seen agents that learn to call search five times on every question because that's what got rewarded, even when the answer was already in their weights.

Then there's the question of how you actually generate rollouts at scale. This is where tool use makes everything harder than standard RLHF. Your rollouts are now slow and asynchronous—you're waiting on a sandbox to execute code, or on an API to return. So you need infrastructure that can run thousands of these interactions in parallel, handle failures gracefully, because tools fail all the time, and then feed those trajectories back into training without the GPUs sitting idle. We spent a lot of time on that decoupling—having the inference and tool execution happen separately from the gradient updates, so you're not bottlenecked on the slowest environment.

And the last thing I'd say is that you have to start with a model that can actually do the task sometimes. RL amplifies what's already there. If the base model has a zero percent success rate on a task, there's no signal to learn from. So we typically do some amount of supervised warm-up on reasonable trajectories—doesn't have to be a lot—just enough that the model knows the format and succeeds often enough that the reward isn't all zeros. Then RL takes it from there, and that's where you see the interesting behaviors emerge: the model learning when not to use a tool, learning to recover from a bad tool result, that kind of thing. Those behaviors are really hard to get through supervised data alone, because you'd have to anticipate every failure mode. With RL, the model discovers them.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by defining what success looks like for the task. The agent is going to make a sequence of decisions: which tool to call, what arguments to pass, how to interpret the result, and whether to take another action or give an answer. Reinforcement learning lets us optimize that whole sequence against the outcome we care about.

A practical starting point is a model that already has some ability to use tools, perhaps through supervised training on demonstrations. Then you let it attempt tasks in an environment, observe the results, and update the policy based on rewards. If you can verify that the task was completed correctly, that’s a useful reward signal. You might also account for the cost of tool calls, but you have to be careful that you don’t incentivize the agent to stop early just to save resources.

The difficult part is credit assignment. If the agent makes ten calls and ultimately fails, which decision caused the failure? And if it succeeds, did it actually solve the problem or exploit a weakness in your reward? So the environment and the evaluation are just as important as the training algorithm. I’d want to test on new tasks and tool failures to see whether it has learned a strategy that generalizes.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is, you’re training the agent to make a sequence of decisions. Given the user’s request, should it call a tool? Which tool should it call, and with what arguments? Then, once it gets the result back, what should it do next?

You need an environment where the agent can actually execute those calls and observe the consequences. You let it attempt a task, collect that trajectory, and assign a reward based on whether it accomplished the task. Reinforcement learning then makes the decisions that led to successful outcomes more likely.

The tricky part is defining success. A tool call can be syntactically correct and still be completely unhelpful. So you want to reward the outcome, rather than just the fact that the agent used a tool. And you may want to account for the cost of getting there—how many calls it made, how long it took—so it learns to use tools efficiently.

There’s also a credit assignment problem. If the agent makes five calls and then fails, which decision was responsible? That’s why the environment and the quality of the feedback matter so much. The training algorithm is one piece, but having tasks you can execute and reliably evaluate is really central.
